title: VibeTraining-Bench: Data-Trainer-Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement
authors: Ruotian Peng, Yuanyi Ren, Shuaiqi Liu et al.
abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) requires agents to diagnose system bottlenecks and coordinate improvements across training and inference. We refer to the agents' capability to jointly optimize training data, the trainer, and the inference harness as cross-component co-design. We introduce VibeTraining-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating this capability across tasks spanning terminal operation, software engineering, multi-turn tool use, and mathematical reasoning. Within each task, research agents

title: DeepSEA: A Multilingual Evaluation Benchmark for Southeast Asia
authors: Jiuzhou Han, Abhishek Bijay Mishra, Trevor Cohn et al.
abstract: While language models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, their performance remains disproportionately skewed towards high-resource languages. This disparity is particularly acute for the 700 million inhabitants of Southeast Asia, where vast linguistic diversity remains under-represented in existing benchmarks, often suffering from limited language coverage or narrow task scopes. To address this, we introduce DeepSEA, a comprehensive benchmark constructed from established datasets through

title: FinHopper: A Progressive Multi-Hop Benchmark for Complex Financial Agents with Step-wise Evaluation
authors: Yuxuan Wu, Miaopei Lin, Qiufang Ying et al.
abstract: Financial agents are expected to answer factual investment queries through open search, but financial multi-hop retrieval differs from general multi-hop QA in a crucial way: each intermediate answer is an exact typed constraint, such as an entity, date, event, or numerical indicator, that determines the next query. title: Scaling Synthetic Pre-training Data and Evaluation for Indic LLMs
authors: Abhinav Khattar, Aishwarya Chhabra, Ameya Velingker et al.
abstract: Building capable language models for India requires scalable multilingual data and robust evaluation. We introduce Nemotron-Pretraining-Indic-v1, a synthetic pretraining corpus of approximately 2.83 trillion tokens covering all 22 scheduled Indian languages in native script and twelve in romanized form. It is the largest openly released Indic pretraining corpus. Using our GPU-accelerated pipeline, we translate curated English documents, assess translation quality, and repair low-quality outputs

title: LOOP: Recovery-Aligned Iterative Layer Pruning via On-Policy Distillation
authors: Liang Xu, Shufan Shen, Zhongni Hou et al.
abstract: Layer-level pruning is attractive for large language model (LLM) deployment as it reduces the model size while preserving a dense architecture that can be efficiently executed on standard hardware. Current methods typically follow a one-shot paradigm, which first removes selected layers to reach a target model size and then performs additional training to recover model capabilities. title: Neither Over- nor Under-Constrained: Evaluating LLM Personalization under a Constraint Qualification Audit
authors: Xuran Li, Guanqin Zhang, Imran Razzak et al.
abstract: Accurate evaluation of LLM personalization is hindered by current evaluation paradigms that over- or under-constrain the response space, yielding frequent false rejections and false acceptances. To reduce these false rates, we introduce ConQual-Audit, an audit-based framework that evaluates LLM personalization through a three-stage process: (1) extracting semantic constraints from user profiles and task-grounded reference; (2) qualifying constraints by pruning unnecessary constraints and recover

title: OPDArena: Understanding Learning and Forgetting in On-Policy Distillation
authors: Yuanze Xu, Tianzhu Ye, Hui Sun et al.
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is increasingly used for language model post-training, yet how teacher supervision shapes learning and forgetting remains unclear. We present OPDArena, a framework comparing supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), and OPD across five pretrained models and diverse teacher sources. It jointly evaluates mathematical learning, general capability retention, and predictive distribution changes. Teacher choice strongly shapes ret

title: Selecting and Composing Agent Design Patterns: Industrial Case Evidence and Controlled Reference-System Experiments
authors: Jia Huang, Bingsheng Ru, Bo Liang et al.
abstract: Agent pattern catalogs describe architectural alternatives, but engineers also need evidence for selecting and composing them. We extend a cognitive-function--execution-topology framework with an evidence-driven selection procedure and explicit composition contracts. The study combines two industrial case accounts, a contributor's collaboration design, seven practitioner workshops, and executable fault-injection experiments. Three local reference systems use SQLite state, shared artifact files,

title: More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents
authors: Ruhan Wang, Kishan Panaganti, Dongruo Zhou
abstract: LLM agents can improve across tasks without updating model parameters by storing experience from their own executions in external memory and reusing it to guide later decisions. A central design question is whether to retain only observed trajectories and outcomes or also the rules, summaries, and skills inferred from them. Retaining these abstractions allows agents to reuse strategies without repeatedly deriving them from raw trajectories. However, errors in stored abstractions can propagate to

title: ProMemAgent: Long-Horizon Proactive Assistance with Context-Aware Prospective Memory from Sensory Perceptions
authors: Lilin Xu, Linyang He, Kaiyuan Hou et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are moving beyond reactive responses toward proactive assistance that anticipates user needs without explicit requests. However, existing proactive agents primarily address immediate needs, while many everyday situations involve delayed intentions that can only be acted on hours or days later. Humans handle such intentions through prospective memory, the ability to remember to act on an intention when the right moment arises. In this paper, we introduce ProMemAg

title: REM: What to Store, When to Recall, What to Forget in Experience Memory for Coding Agents
authors: Xinyi Lisa Chen, Pedro Herrero-Vidal, Xiaohan Chen et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents now autonomously complete long-horizon tasks, such as repository-level coding, through hundreds of think-act steps, yet the experience each run produces is rarely reused on the next. Prior memory systems concentrate on retrieval, finding the most relevant past trajectory. title: An LLM-Based Agent for Legal Compliance Assessment: Architecture, Memory, and Evaluation in a Canadian and Quebec Context
authors: Soukaina Alaoui Ismaili, Jean-Sebastien Dessureault
abstract: Checking whether a text complies with a body of law is slow when done by hand and fragile when done with keyword rules. This paper presents ComplianceAgent, the legal compliance sub-agent of COMPASS, a multi-agent framework that evaluates texts along four axes: digital sovereignty, carbon impact, compliance, and ethics. The agent relies on a large language model that scores a text on a fixed rubric, grounds its judgment in a reference legal corpus, and, when the score falls at or below a critica

title: Evolving Self-tuning Benchmarks for Long-Horizon Tool Use
authors: Hyunji Alex Nam, Michael Dennis, Natasha Jaques et al.
abstract: For AI assistants to move beyond simple chat interfaces and reliably assist users with applications like Gmail, Venmo, and Slack, we need to improve their tool-use capabilities. However, existing tool use benchmarks are still limited and difficult to scale because they rely on human supervision or are too domain-specific. title: Evaluating Context Compaction on the Questions That Come Later
authors: Junwei Yao, Yongxi Zhou, Zike Yang et al.
abstract: Language-model agents compact their context for the question at hand, but the compacted context must also serve questions that come later. We evaluate compaction on these later questions, using four corpora that annotate the evidence of several questions per text and recorded agent trajectories, and compare every method with random deletion at the same budget. title: RealControlBench: A Benchmark for Interpretability-Informed Fine-Grained Control of LLMs and Agents
authors: Xinying Cai, Bin Hu, Mingyu Jin et al.
abstract: Existing steering benchmarks are built around simplified, isolated generation tasks and evaluate a single behavioral attribute under controlled settings that do not reflect the diversity and complexity of practical deployment. As a result, performance on these benchmarks provides only a limited picture of how steering methods perform in the real world. We therefore introduce RealControlBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating fine-grained steering of LLMs and LLM agents across diverse beh

title: EGI-BENCH: An Enterprise General Intelligence Benchmark Suite
authors: Zhiwei Liu, Zhujun Lan, Jielin Qiu et al.
abstract: Enterprise adoption of LLMs in agentic workflows is gated by evaluations that span a wide arc of abilities: CRM operations, heterogeneous-document retrieval, personal data understanding, multi-turn planning, tool use, function calling, long-horizon research, and long-context software engineering. These evaluations live today in separate repositories with divergent runners, dependencies, and scoring conventions, which makes cross-benchmark comparison difficult and obscures what a single aggregate

title: Magnolia: A Persistent-Memory Agent Framework for Computational Chemistry
authors: Tao Jiang, Benjamin Navet, Yousouf Taghzouti et al.
abstract: Chemistry has recently entered a high-data regime as molecular databases from high-throughput platforms or computational studies have become available. Increasing automation within the chemical sciences leads to a more digital and precision chemistry. Dedicated scientific agents are becoming central to guiding the chemist through an ever-increasing amount of data and findings, including negative ones. Here, we introduce Magnolia, a persistent-memory artificial intelligence agent framework that i

title: Which Agent's Skill Should Change? Group-Relative Credit Assignment for Evolving Multi-Agent Teams
authors: Yanan Ma, Yang Wang, David Le et al.
abstract: Cooperative language-model agents can improve without weight updates by revising reusable skills, but only if a shared team reward is traced to the responsible agent and skill. Existing methods credit the skills present in each trajectory, yet presence is not responsibility: a harmful skill active in successful runs still earns positive credit. title: PORA: Learning When More Reasoning Pays Off for LLM Agents
authors: Bo Yan, Qi Zhang, Zhen Tan et al.
abstract: LLM agents perform tasks over multiple steps and revise their actions based on feedback. As the total reasoning budget is often limited and must support future steps, the agent must choose between short and long reasoning before each action. Longer reasoning may improve the final task outcome by preventing later errors, but it also uses budget capacity that may be needed for future decisions. title: PROVISO: Provenance-Informed Action Selection for Secure LLM Agents
authors: Bo Yan, Qi Zhang, Ziwen Kan et al.
abstract: LLM agents act on the external world through tools and third-party skills, so a single executed action can cause irreversible harm. Existing defenses judge a proposed action without tracking whether its content comes from the user or from external sources such as tool outputs, and they judge it in isolation rather than against an available alternative, which forces a trade-off between security and utility. title: A general-purpose System One decision model for clinical records
authors: Andrew Zhang, Trinh T. L. Vuong, Sophia J. Wagner et al.
abstract: Clinical care, health-system operations and biomedical discovery depend on extracting reliable answers from patient records, yet applying diverse clinical questions across entire populations remains computationally expensive. Here we present Clinical System One (CS1), a 4-billion-parameter decision model for fast, typed judgments from clinical records, along with two agentic harnesses in which CS1 works together with a generalist language model. CS1-4B is trained on 12.4 million questions and an

title: M-Plan: Comprehensive Planning For LLM Agents with Memory Arrangement
authors: Ziyang Liu, Jiakang Yuan, Jiayuan Fan et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents have recently demonstrated outstanding performance in single-turn tasks, yet they continue to struggle with long-horizon tasks, particularly in environments without prior training. A key limitation of single LLMs is their difficulty in processing long contexts, which stems from weaknesses in continuous decision-making and reasoning capabilities. Although existing multi-agent systems (MAS) equipped with long-term memory bases can partially address this gap,

title: SPEM: Structure-Aware Procedural Memory for Efficient Skill Use in LLM Agents
authors: Ran Zhou, Zehui Kong, Fanyu Lin et al.
abstract: LLM-based agents increasingly rely on reusable skills. However, scaling skill libraries makes efficient and accurate skill use difficult. Full skill loading incurs high token and runtime overhead. In contrast, flat semantic retrieval treats skills as independent text entries, ignoring dependencies, execution order, state transitions, and data flow constraints. title: DStill: Trajectory Consistency Distillation for Accelerated One-Step Drafting in Block Diffusion Speculative Decoding
authors: Shreyas Kulkarni, Uttam Gurram, Madhav Kanda et al.
abstract: Block-diffusion speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by drafting multiple tokens in parallel. However, one-step drafting in discrete diffusion is limited by token factorization error: each token is predicted from the same masked block, without conditioning on the tokens selected at other positions in that step. title: Sparse RL Relaxation for LLM Reasoning
authors: Jiabin Fan, Matthias Lindemann, Zita Marinho et al.
abstract: Recent work has explored continuous representations in place of discrete tokens during Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, often referred to as soft CoT. This is motivated by the idea that a mixture of token embeddings can represent a superposition of multiple reasoning possibilities within a single step. title: Understanding the Benefits of Scaffolds through Computational Separations
authors: Jingchu Gai, Adam Block, Andrej Risteski
abstract: Inference-time harnesses, i.e., external procedures that call a model many times and keep state across calls, can substantially improve model capabilities. In this paper, we investigate the benefits of using such harnesses and the extent to which these benefits can be internalized through training. More precisely, we conceptualize a harness $\mathcal{A}$ as an arbitrary wrapper around a base model $M$ and attempt to distill a student model from the harness's traces. title: ICLHerd: Herding-Based Data Selection for LLMs with In-Context Learning as a Proxy
authors: Yuqiao Wen, Lili Mou
abstract: Data selection plays a central role in modern large language model training, as the quality of training data strongly influences downstream performance. A common approach is to curate a development set that encodes the desired skills (e.g., reasoning or multilinguality) and select data that are similar to them. title: EDMA: Entropy-Driven Multimodal Answering
authors: Emanuele Mezzi, Gertjan Burghouts, Fabio Massacci et al.
abstract: Multimodal question answering (MMQA) is based on integrating heterogeneous data sources, selectively leveraging relevant modalities, and ignoring distractors. Existing approaches based on Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) improve performance by splitting the task into intermediate steps, but do not quantify how each modality contributes to reaching the final answer. We argue that quantifying the effect that each modality has on the answering process improves process traceability and final

title: Cross-Lingual Reusability of LLM Pipelines: Financial Extraction, Multilingual Reasoning, and Semantic Screening
authors: Joong Ho,  Choi, Sherine George et al.
abstract: Financial institutions increasingly deploy large language models (LLMs) in multilingual markets, raising a practical question: can pipelines developed and validated in English be reused across languages, or must they be rebuilt per locale? We test cross-lingual reusability along three dimensions--accuracy, reasoning-effort transfer, and behavioural stability--through three complementary tasks. title: Fluent but Fallible: Benchmarking Hallucination and Factual Reliability in Large Language Models
authors: Osama Shabih, Dayam Nadeem, Shahab Saquib Sohail et al.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have significantly advanced natural language processing and artificial intelligence applications through their capabilities in reasoning, text generation and knowledge retrieval. However, LLMs are still vulnerable to two important challenges: hallucination, generating factually incorrect or fabricated content, and response deviation, meaning systematic deviations from ground-truth responses. title: On the Limits of Scale: Inverse Scaling in Vision-Language Models
authors: Rohit Saxena, Alessandro Suglia, Marek Rei et al.
abstract: Scaling laws suggest that increasing model size, training data, and compute generally yields monotonic performance improvements. While this often holds at the aggregate level, we present systematic evidence that vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit inverse scaling at the subtask level: specific question categories on which larger models perform worse than smaller counterparts within the same model family. We evaluate 19 models from four distinct model families across eight multimodal benchmarks

title: CARLAR Influence: A Structured Hallucination Risk in Multimodal Cheque Extraction and an Exploratory Compressed-Image Countermeasure
authors: Joong Ho,  Choi, Aditya Paul et al.
abstract: Multimodal large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for structured extraction from financial documents, but their behavior under visual ambiguity is poorly understood. We study CARLAR (Courtesy Amount Recognition and Legal Amount Recognition) influence: a model returns the same amount for both cheque fields even though their annotations differ, including cases with a blank annotation encoded as zero. Across ten visual prompting conditions, we evaluate GPT-4.1 and Claude 4.5 Sonnet on 2

title: TxnQA: Benchmarking Analytical Reasoning and Evidence Grounding over Transaction Event Sequences
authors: Rabimba Karanjai, Yiming Bian, Yun-Shiuan Chuang et al.
abstract: Analyzing merchant transaction histories requires dynamic temporal filtering, entity resolution, and aggregation over irregular event streams--operations poorly captured by static tabular or time-series forecasting benchmarks. We introduce TxnQA, an analytical QA benchmark comprising 27 task families (81 templates) alongside a 5-scenario fraud-risk reasoning suite that evaluates both verdicts and supporting evidence over synthetic, privacy-mitigated transaction data. Ground-truth answers are com

title: LSA-PAST: Layer-Specific Adaptation and Prototype Transport for Compositional Incremental Learning
authors: Kyle Stein, Andrew Arash Mahyari, Guillermo Francia et al.
abstract: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) enables models to recognize new classes over time while retaining prior knowledge, but many real-world problems are compositional, where visual concepts arise from combinations of primitives such as states (i.e., red, shiny) and objects (i.e., shoe, car). Standard CIL methods treat each composition as an independent class, ignoring shared primitives and providing no mechanism to stabilize their representations as new compositions arrive. title: Evaluating Tibetan Speech Recognition Across Dialects and Adaptation Regimes: A Multi-Granularity Analysis
authors: Jacob Moore, Sheng Li
abstract: Tibetan speech recognition is usually evaluated with character or syllable error rates because the writing system does not mark word boundaries. These metrics can rank systems differently and respond differently to adaptation failures. We combine character error rate, syllable error rate, and segmented word error rate in one evaluation framework. title: Fundamental Impossibility Results in AI Safety: Trading Off between Desiderata
authors: Ida Mattsson, Ratip Emin Berker, Emanuel Tewolde et al.
abstract: Is there a fundamental tradeoff between desiderata for safe AI systems, such as harmlessness and helpfulness? We answer by formalizing the interaction between AI systems and users as a game with three players: a defender and an attacker that are computationally or informationally bounded, and an AI that provides public advice and is less constrained. title: Steering Vision-Language Models for Visual-Contextual Privacy in Location Disclosure
authors: Wenyue Chen, Yuhan Cheng, Ruixin Yang et al.
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can infer sensitive information such as geolocation from subtle visual cues, creating privacy risks when responses disclose more detail than the visual context warrants. We study visual-contextual privacy in geolocation disclosure, where a VLM should reveal location information only at the granularity appropriate to the visual context depicted in the image. We first show that this contextually appropriate granularity is recoverable from pre-generation hidden states,

title: Global Security Blind Spots: Translation as a Safety Bypass in Low-Resource Languages
authors: Jalil Alva, David Harper, Abigail E. Thornton et al.
abstract: Large language models are deployed globally, yet safety alignment and evaluation remain concentrated in English: harmful requests refused in English can elicit unsafe completions when translated into low-resource languages. We evaluate ten widely deployed LLMs across 79 languages (English plus 78 low-resource) under a translation-bypass threat model, using a metric conditioned on English safety, which separates translation bypass from unsafety already present in English. English safety does not

title: African Languages AI Safety Readiness Report
authors: Israel Abebe Azime, Jesujoba O. Alabi, Tajuddeen Gwadabe et al.
abstract: With the widespread adoption of large language models (LLMs) across languages and domains, AI safety has emerged as a critical global concern. However, due to resource constraints, research and development efforts tend to prioritize a limited number of high-resource languages, leaving many others, especially those spoken in Africa, underrepresented. While existing research on language "resource-ness" has largely examined whether sufficient resources are available to develop language technologies

title: Auditing Safety Preference Supervision with Recorded Derivations
authors: Chenhan Lyu, Amir Rahmani
abstract: Preference labels align model training, but the judgments behind them are difficult to inspect or verify. In this paper, we examine how preference construction can be checked when intermediate decisions are recorded, and which of them remain uncertain. We present Symbolic Preference Labeling, a method in which a pretrained language model classifies predefined attributes of prompts and responses. Explicit rules assign response verdicts, and a fixed verdict ranking determines the preference label.

title: The Culture Within: Towards Mechanistic Understanding of Cultural Reasoning in LLMs
authors: Samee Arif, Furkan Danisman, Angana Borah et al.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly operate across culturally diverse settings, yet existing evaluations largely measure cultural behavior at the output level. We introduce CultureLens, a reference-grounded benchmark and mechanistic study of how LLMs use cultural information. CultureLens contains 9,261 scenarios across 75 countries and systematically varies country, value, true-norm, and contradictory-norm evidence. title: Exposing Vulnerability Monoculture Through Systemic Adversarial Robustness
authors: Leo Elmecker-Plakolm, Lukasz Szpruch, Avishek Joey Bose et al.
abstract: Beneath the apparent diversity of foundation models lies an increasingly homogeneous technical stack of common training pipelines, distillation methods, and data. These shared algorithmic choices can expose an otherwise distinct model ecosystem to concentrated risks leading to a vulnerability monoculture. title: Generalizing Multimodal Foundational Models in Context-Driven Class Incremental Learning
authors: Avi Gupta, Nilotpal Sinha, Vishnu Raj et al.
abstract: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) aims to learn new classes continuously without forgetting the previously learned ones. Recent works in CIL have significantly advanced across various modalities; however, at the intersection of audio-visual modality, this problem remains underexplored. While representations from multimodal foundational models (MFMs) encapsulate rich static priors, our preliminary analysis shows that these representations struggle in incremental settings. Motivated by this, we pro

title: Stronger artificial intelligence breakthroughs hasten their own exhaustion
authors: Beichen Lu, Honglin Bao, Qi Huang et al.
abstract: Progress in artificial intelligence is widely assumed to scale with effort: more researchers, papers and investment should accelerate discovery. Theories of technological growth instead locate the difficulty of discovery in the space of ideas. Here we show that neither scale nor space is enough: breakthroughs depend on diverse attention, which collective concentration can deplete. title: When Models Know but Can't Linearly Say: Relational Encoding Limits Linear Vulnerability Classification in Code LLMs
authors: Rui Melo, Andre Catarino, Claudia Mamede et al.
abstract: Large language models can detect vulnerable code, yet the form of vulnerability encoding in their representations remains unclear. We analyze 8 code models spanning 6.7B-15B parameters on C programs using three datasets (DELTASECOMMITS, SVEN, and PRECISE-BUGS), comparing two diagnostic tasks on the same representations: identifying what patterns the code instantiates, and determining whether it is vulnerable. title: Target-Aware Curation of Hallucination Stress Tests for Large Language Models
authors: Jiho Lee, Bingquan Zhang, Lin Ting Liang et al.
abstract: Hallucination stress tests can yield similar average scores across language models even when different prompts elicit hallucinations in each model. We develop a procedure that iteratively edits source-grounded seed prompts to expose hallucinations in a target model. An LLM editor revises each prompt in response to the target's answer and a judge's category-specific score and explanation. In the main setting, the target also receives feedback on its previous response. Experiments cover 500 seeds

title: Diagnostic Analysis for Large Language Model Reasoning
authors: Xinyu Liu, Dongqi Fu, Jun Wu
abstract: Reasoning structures (e.g., chains and graphs) are increasingly used for probabilistic inference, factuality verification, and uncertainty estimation, but their structural reliability is rarely evaluated directly. We test whether this reliability holds through a proposed two-stage diagnostic evaluation in open-ended multi-hop QA. Stage 1 tests different capabilities required to construct reasoning graphs, showing that graph reliability varies with topology, prompt design, and model family. Stage

title: Profile-DP: Differential Privacy for User-Controlled Profile Release in Personalized LLM Inference
authors: Mingchen Li, Zifan Peng, Kewei Sha et al.
abstract: Personalized large language models (LLMs) increasingly rely on profile-conditioned inference, pairing public requests with rich, user-specific facts. This paradigm exposes the user profile itself, together with the user's explicit sharing preferences. We introduce Profile-DP, a policy-aware local differential privacy framework designed specifically for user-profile release in personalized LLM inference. title: Preference-Aware Pareto Steering for Multi-Task Speech LLMs
authors: Liuyuan Jiang, Vishal Sunder, Samuel Thomas et al.
abstract: Speech large language models (LLMs) perform multiple tasks, including automatic speech recognition (ASR), timestamp prediction (TS), and speech translation (ST). Joint training of speech LLMs creates task trade-offs, yet standard training with fixed loss weights does not generally control the resulting trade-off according to deployment preferences. title: Visual Task Modeling and Automated Planning for Humanoid Robots in Education of Individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder
authors: Lada Kudláčková
abstract: In robot-assisted education, a robot must understand how to complete a task in order to effectively guide a student through it. We present a novel method that enables a semi-autonomous, camera-equipped robot to recognise the task goal and plan actions to achieve it. Our work focuses on Shoebox Tasks, an activity commonly used in the education of individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). These tasks are designed so that the goal can be inferred directly from their visual structure. We have

title: ClockMark: Adaptive and Host-Dependent Watermarking for Large Language Models
authors: Yupeng Qiu, Han Fang, Ee-Chien Chang
abstract: Large language model (LLM) watermarking operates on the next-token distribution that evolves during generation. In streaming generation, each sampled token becomes part of the text and affects subsequent distributions. Embedding therefore proceeds with a changing host, unlike classical watermarking, which adapts embedding to an existing host signal. title: Discrete Neural Interlingua for Ontology-Agnostic EHR Modeling
authors: Tong Ding, Caiwei Tian, Dongmin Bang et al.
abstract: EHR foundation models promise scalable clinical prediction across health systems, yet their deployment is constrained by a tokenization bottleneck. The same clinical concept can appear as different ontology codes, local identifiers, synonyms, or free-text descriptions, which standard EHR tokenizers treat as unrelated symbols. title: Physical AI: Concepts, Techniques, and Challenges
authors: Weinan Zhang, Chunhua Shen, Tianfan Xue et al.
abstract: In recent years, physical artificial intelligence (physical AI) has experienced rapid development, capturing significant attention in academia and industry. However, the field has yet to reach consensus on its definition, technical landscape, and core challenges. To address this gap, this monograph seeks to define physical AI, present its technical landscape, and examine each key technical subfield in depth. title: From Outcomes to Components: A Counterfactual Evaluation Framework for LLM-Proposed Repairs
authors: Hengyu Ye, Songhua Hu
abstract: A repair action proposed by a large language model (LLM) specifies which records to change and how to change their values. A failed action may still contain a useful choice of records or a useful update, depending on how the two are paired. We introduce a counterfactual evaluation framework that separates selected records (targets) from the applied change (an update). title: TEX: Test-Time Scaling Testing Agents via Execution-based Cross-Validation
authors: Akash Gokul, Srijan Bansal, Yingbo Zhou et al.
abstract: Test-case generation is critical but remains challenging for language models. Existing test-time scaling methods either isolate candidates or aggregate traces, which do not scale to long-horizon tasks. We present TEX, a collaborative test-time scaling framework based on execution-driven cross-validation. title: Guided Diffusion for Trustworthy Synthetic Text Generation
authors: Qi Pang, Hanshen Xiao, Andre Manoel et al.
abstract: The rapid evolution of Large Language Models is fueled by massive datasets, yet this reliance poses severe privacy risks, as models can inadvertently memorize and even directly output sensitive training data. Synthetic text generation offers a promising solution to this challenge; however, existing methods struggle to reconcile rigorous privacy guarantees with high data utility. title: Teaching AI Agent to Play Poker Strategically Through Preference Optimization
authors: Phurinat Polasa, Thanapon Thanadunpremdet, Phatthanasak Kraiduang et al.
abstract: A poker agent can make a legal move and still make a strategically poor one. We ask whether compact AI agents can exhibit strategic behavior under hidden information and whether preference optimization can improve beyond static and zero-shot policies. title: Benchmark for Structured Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Perovskite Photovoltaics
authors: Qiwei Han, Chi Zhou, Gaoxiang Yuan
abstract: While retrieval-augmented language models increasingly serve as literature assistants in the physical sciences, existing benchmarks evaluate them primarily on qualitative text overlap or through model-based scoring rather than against verified experimental ground truth. title: Aligning Language Models with Indigenous Community Cosmovision through Constitutional AI
authors: Silvia Fernández-Sabido, Jorge Reyes-Magaña, Jesús Adrián Chay Tun et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are predominantly trained on corpora that reflect Western, anglophone worldviews. This asymmetry is not neutral: when a model answers questions about territory, community authority, or the relationship with nature, it does so from assumptions that may be alien to the communities using the system. title: Toward Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Enterprise Retail Workflows over Heterogeneous Data Sources
authors: Jeonghwan Choi, Jibin Hwang, Hayoon Park et al.
abstract: Enterprise retail workflows require agents to chain evidence across heterogeneous sources, from structured product and order records to unstructured inquiries and reviews, yet existing agentic RAG benchmarks rarely capture this challenge. To enable controlled evaluation of such workflows, we introduce RetailBridge, a compositional retail benchmark built from persona-driven simulations. title: The World as Viewed by 136 Countries: An Open, Curated, Annotated, and Multilingual Dataset of 118 Million State Media Articles
authors: Bryan Li, Samar Haider, Grace Kim et al.
abstract: State media outlets often project their governments' narratives to target both domestic and foreign audiences. Because this content is plentiful and free to access, it appears widely in the web corpora that large language models (LLMs) are trained on and that retrieval systems draw from. However, the prevalence of state media in these corpora and its potential influence on LLM outputs remain largely unexplored. title: Design and Cross-Domain Evaluation of an Agent Execution Harness
authors: Saurav Joshi, Manas Gupta, Ashwin Venkatesh Raman et al.
abstract: Completing complex tasks with language-model agents requires coordinating planning, execution, and review so the final result addresses the user's original objective. We present an agent execution harness that keeps the original objective separate from a revisable plan and an execution record. A planner assigns scoped tasks, workers produce outputs and artifacts, and a reviewer examines results against the original request before submitting or requesting additional work. title: Learning Which Device to Call: Online Tool Grounding for LLM Agents in IoT
authors: Yichen Liu, Xiaochong Jiang, Haoran Yu et al.
abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) gives large language model (LLM) agents access to physical observations, but one requested capability is usually offered by several devices, and the agent's plan does not say which one to call. Existing work retrieves relevant tools and checks plan feasibility, without learning which eligible device returns a useful observation. title: Symbolic Constraint Agents: Mining Formal Tool-Call Constraints to Prevent Agent Errors
authors: Jinu Lee, Shraddha Barke
abstract: Symbolic constraints (programmatic, deterministic checks for tool calls) enable deterministic verification of LLM agents' tool calls, but existing approaches primarily enforce predefined safety policies rather than tool dependencies in complex tool environments. We explore whether symbolic constraints can be mined from environments and observations beyond predefined policies, and whether they can improve end-to-end task performance. title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
authors: Yunlong Deng, Yan Li, Xing Hu et al.
abstract: A synopsis in novels folds a story into a few lines; a function in code gathers many steps with a single execution. Context editing is native to language itself. In this paper, we propose the Native Context Editing (NCE) framework, which gives language model agents a grammar for natively editing their own context. title: Outcome-Anchored Credit Reallocation for Agentic Knowledge Graph Question Answering
authors: Mingyuan Li, Yucheng Li, Xiaxia Wang et al.
abstract: Agentic knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) requires large language models (LLMs) to solve complex questions through multi-turn interactions with a knowledge graph (KG). title: Bridging Concepts: Multi-Agent Reasoning over Scientific Concept Graphs for High-Impact Research Prediction
authors: Donggyu Yoon, Minsung Hwang, Juneha Baek et al.
abstract: Within a research community, new topics often emerge when previously unconnected concepts are first studied together. We construct scientific concept graphs (SCGs)--domain knowledge graphs whose nodes are fine-grained research concepts extracted from paper text by LLMs and whose edges capture their co-occurrence in papers--and study the task of forecasting high-impact concept pairs, i.e., discovering concept pairs that are currently unconnected but will have high impact when connected. title: Dialogue Generation for Conversational Recommendation Using User Search Interactions and Knowledge Graphs
authors: Minsung Hwang, Donggyu Yoon, Gowoon Hwang et al.
abstract: Large-scale conversational recommendation datasets typically require manual dialogue construction or annotation. We propose SearCl, which automatically generates conversational recommendation dialogues grounded in user search and click behaviors. SearCl segments user interactions into query sessions and derives each recommendation target from content selected after a search query. title: Indistinguishable Agents: Training Agent Privacy as Twin-World Indistinguishability
authors: Jiaming He, Guanyu Hou, Yi Yu et al.
abstract: LLM agents search, shop and send messages for their users, and every action is seen by some party. Existing privacy training rewards agents for not mentioning protected items, yet an observer can infer a private fact from what the agent does. Since an observer learns a fact only if its view changes with the fact, we propose \methodfull (\method), which trains on twin worlds that differ only in the private fact. title: Trackable Skill Library Lifecycle Management for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
authors: Xi Zhu, Yuanlin Duan, Changyi Yang et al.
abstract: Skill-augmented agentic RL has emerged as an effective approach to improving LLM agents on long-horizon tasks. Despite this progress, individual skills may follow distinct trajectories as the policy evolves, with some becoming redundant after the model internalizes their capabilities, others remaining valuable as external scaffolding, and still others turning harmful. title: Memories That Outlive Their Reasons: Dependency-Tethered Memory for Tool-Using LLM Agents
authors: Yiqi Wang, Jinqian Ju, Jiaqi Zhang et al.
abstract: Agents now act on the Web, publishing packages, models and datasets through registry APIs, and remembering past verifications spares them the work. But a verdict rests on premises. When a signing key is revoked, everything built on it stops passing, yet the advisory names only the key, and the old verdicts of its dependents may never share a retrieval window with it. title: Explore or Confirm? LLM Agents Misallocate Measurements Under Noise
authors: Abdul Karim, Matt Keon
abstract: As model reasoning gets cheaper, the physical experiment becomes the slow and costly step in discovery. Each experiment returns a noisy reading: a high value can mean a good candidate or a lucky draw. With a fixed budget, an AI agent must keep choosing between exploring a new candidate and confirming a promising one by re-testing it. title: LLM Agents as Suppliers of Physical System Models: Calibration and Acceptance in Modelica
authors: Jörg Frochte, Herbert Schmidt
abstract: To procure a model of a device, a client hands a supplier a description, sometimes with recorded data or a target response, and accepts the model against this handover. We let LLM coding agents act as the supplier on handovers with data, building Modelica models from library components for four simulated systems and a real switching magnet, and ask what acceptance certifies. title: CorrectRTL: Boost RTL Generation Quality Through Automated Self-Correction with Instruction Decomposition
authors: Jing Wang, Shang Liu, Hangan Zhou et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong promise in specification-to-RTL generation. Among the explorations, the self-correction paradigm has significantly advanced LLM-based RTL generation. However, two challenges limit further progress. Existing benchmarks are saturated by advanced LLMs, leaving little room to evaluate the agentic self-correction framework. title: MemPrice: Online Memory Allocation via Adaptive Pricing for Long-Horizon Agents
authors: Yiming Zong, Shiyuan Piao, Jiashuo Jiang et al.
abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents face a fundamental allocation problem as interaction histories grow: which information to retain, how much context to devote to it, and at what granularity. Existing memory mechanisms largely focus on relevance, retrieval, or compression, leaving this allocation trade-off implicit. title: TrustAgent-RFF: Agentic Diagnostic Planning for Reliable RF Fingerprinting under Domain Shift
authors: Chuan Liu, Tianya Zhao, Xuyu Wang
abstract: Radio frequency fingerprinting (RFF) models can achieve accuracy under source domain conditions but become unreliable when the receiver, distance, collection day, or environment changes. Incorrect predictions in unseen domains may receive high softmax confidence, making confidence thresholding insufficient for trustworthy deployment. title: ATEST: Adaptive Resource-Aware Test-Time Scaling for LLM Inference
authors: Mobina Kashaniyan, Ali Jannesari
abstract: Test-time scaling (TTS) improves large language model (LLM) reasoning by sampling multiple answers, but fixed sampling budgets ignore both query difficulty and the changing energy cost of inference under GPU contention. We measure up to a 4.1-fold increase in energy for the same four-sample query as GPU load rises. title: Formal Raising: Embedding Verifiable Ethical Properties into the Development of AI
authors: Rolf Drechsler, Christina Plump
abstract: Alan Turing proposed constructing a ``child machine'' and educating it rather than directly programming an adult-like intelligent machine. Recent work on model raising revives this developmental view for Large Language Models by arguing that moral values should accompany capability acquisition from the beginning rather than be added only through post-hoc alignment. title: System X: An LLM Decision Model That Replies from Its Own KV Cache
authors: Syed Usama Khalid Bukhari, Syed Safwan Khalid, Muhammad Aamir
abstract: Decision models return probabilities over supplied options, but a deployed agent may also need to reply in words. The present study introduces System X, a large language model (LLM) decision model that adds a text-reply option to the LLM-as-Jev readout. When this option wins, or confidence is low, the same model continues from the decision's key-value (KV) cache, avoiding a repeated prompt prefill. authors: Yifei Shi, Michalis Korakakis, Rami Aly et al.
abstract: Verifying the reasoning of large language models is increasingly important as they are applied to complex mathematical and scientific problems. Existing work focuses on large decoder models and reports mixed results for generative and discriminative verifiers, leaving unclear which paradigm is more effective and whether large models are necessary. title: When Form Changes but Logic Doesn't: Building Logic-invariant LLMs through Logical Structure
authors: Xuyuan Liu, Xinshuai Dong, Elynn Chen et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance across diverse reasoning tasks, yet it remains unclear whether this performance reflects an understanding of underlying logical structure or a reliance on shallow semantic cues. title: From Unverifiable Domain Text to Cross-Lingual RLVR via Code-Switched Task Synthesis
authors: Cheonbok Park, Jihwan Kim, Shinyoung Joo et al.
abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) can improve reasoning in large language models, but specialized non-English domains expose a data mismatch. Raw English domain text is often available, while target-language RLVR tasks with verifiable rewards are scarce. We introduce code-switched task synthesis for cross-lingual RLVR, a data-centric approach that derives target-language and code-switched RLVR task variants from otherwise unverifiable English domain text. title: Where and Why Search-Augmented LLMs Fail When Reasoning over Rapidly Evolving Knowledge
authors: Tianyi Hu, Bhavyajeet Singh, Niket Tandon et al.
abstract: As the world changes, new information is published while older records remain online. This complicates reasoning for large language models (LLMs), which must retrieve evidence and resolve conflicts to determine which information remains valid. Existing evaluations treat information seeking as a black box, revealing little about where and why LLMs fail. title: Calibration-Free Early Stopping for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning via E-processes
authors: Dong-Jae Lee, Gyojin Han, Junmo Kim
abstract: Reasoning large language models (LLMs) benefit from test-time scaling, motivating adaptive policies that spend tokens when they help and stop early otherwise. Existing rules halt when a confidence or stability signal crosses a threshold, but such thresholds rarely transfer across models and datasets, and validation-calibrated rules lose their guarantee under shifts in test-time horizon or signal dynamics. title: TIRE: Top-Down Formula Instantiation with Reliable Execution for Physics Problem Synthesis
authors: Xiaoyu Wu, Zhaoxin Yu, Xinglin Xiao et al.
abstract: Advancing physics reasoning in large language models requires scalable training data that connect physical laws, concrete problem scenarios, and verifiable numerical answers. Expert-designed problems offer top-down control over physical laws, conditions, and scenarios, but require costly human effort. title: Beyond Factual Accuracy: A Benchmark for Evaluating Perspective Alignment in LLMs
authors: Sunghoon Kim, Sangyeop Kim
abstract: Large Language Models often generate factually correct responses that fail to maintain user-requested perspectives, blending multiple perspectives and forcing users to filter through unwanted information---a perspective control failure that factual accuracy metrics cannot detect. title: ReTrace: Visual Backtracking for Efficient Multimodal Large Language Models
authors: Guangzong Si, Dong Wang, Yifan Yu et al.
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) encode images into dense visual token sequences, creating substantial attention and KV-cache overhead. Existing visual token compression methods reduce this cost by pruning low-saliency tokens in shallow layers, but this practice couples temporary computational deactivation with irreversible information deletion. title: DeGMatch: Target-Aware Reasoning Data Selection via Deconfounded Gradient Matching
authors: Changho Lee, Janghoon Han, Rajdeep Mukherjee et al.
abstract: Reasoning post-training on long trajectories has substantially improved the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but scaling such training to large datasets is increasingly expensive. We study target-aware reasoning data selection, where a small reference set specifies a target capability and guides the selection of training trajectories for specialization. title: CasePlay: Self-Play Reinforcement Learning from Case Reports for Medical Reasoning
authors: Hao Wang, Zihan Wang, Kai Wu et al.
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a promising way to improve the clinical reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs), but current pipelines often rely on expert-labeled questions or costly synthetic-data generation. title: A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help
authors: Shashwat Singh, He He, Tal Linzen
abstract: Vision-language (VL) models are typically built by fine-tuning a language model to attend to visual features in service of a Visual Question-Answering objective. We ask whether this alignment changes how language models represent text---especially on tasks where visualization would help, like geometry questions posed in words. title: ViCoR: Estimating Visual Necessity via Counterfactual Residuals for Multimodal Medical Data Selection
authors: Haotian Gan, Yudong Li, Xintian Li et al.
abstract: Medical vision-language models often exhibit hidden stratification, where high overall performance masks failures on subtle visual findings and overlapping clinical conditions. title: Multimodal-Conditioned Latent Diffusion Models for Spatiotemporal Brain MRI Forecasting
authors: Antonio Scardace, Silvia Ingala, Sebastiano Battiato et al.
abstract: Spatiotemporal forecasting of 3D anatomical changes is a critical generative vision challenge for modeling Alzheimer's Disease (AD) progression. While brain MRI forecasting from single-modality data has advanced, other key complementary multimodal biomarkers remain underutilized. In this work, we propose the Multimodal-Conditioned Latent Diffusion Model (MC-LDM), a novel framework for patient-specific brain MRI synthesis. authors: Jiaqi Gan, Tsang Ng, Ankit Raj et al.
abstract: Small language models have improved to the point where a phone can plausibly screen its own calls, answering on an absent owner's behalf without sending call content off the device, a privacy-respecting alternative to cloud call handling. title: Aligning Cultural Behaviors in Arabic Language Models via Preferences
authors: Junhong Liang, Daniil Orel, Saeed Almheiri et al.
abstract: Arabic LLMs have improved rapidly, but aligning them with country-specific cultural behavioral preferences remains underexplored. Previous work has focused primarily on instruction-tuning for factual knowledge, overlooking nuanced cultural behaviors. authors: Hans Peter Lyngsøe Raaschou-jensen, M. Onurcan Kaya, Desmond Elliott
abstract: Recent test-time scaling methods improve model performance by increasing inference-time compute. One practical form of this is parallel scaling, where a model samples multiple independent reasoning streams and aggregates their answers using methods like voting, reranking, or verification. title: Hidden Cartographer: Hidden State Guided Data Selection for Dual Budgeted Instruction Tuning
authors: Zixuan Qin, Qi Qin, Erbo Li et al.
abstract: Given the high cost of expert annotation and limited fine-tuning resources, effective data selection from large unlabeled pools under strict budgets has become a crucial step in adapting LLMs to specialized domains. Existing label-dependent methods risk distorted selection when using pseudo-labels, while traditional active learning methods do not explicitly characterize instruction-tuning dynamics. title: PLANE: Plug-and-Play Fine-Grained Visual Experts for Hallucination Mitigation in Large Vision-Language Models
authors: Jianghao Yin, Lang Yu, Qianxi Yu et al.
abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) commonly suffer from hallucinations, which appear as fabricating non-existent objects or outputting incorrect attributes and spatial relationships in images. Previous works empirically indicate that CLIP-style vision encoders tend to focus on primary objects while ignoring image details, which is one of the causes of hallucinations. title: Robust Direct Preference Optimization under Preference Label-Flip Attacks
authors: Chenye Yang, Weiyu Xu, Lifeng Lai
abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is widely used for offline Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback. However, recent works have shown that DPO can be easily manipulated by adversarial preference label flip attacks, which are specifically designed to mislead the learner toward an attacker-chosen target policy. authors: Jaehong Myung, Seunghun Oh, Unsang Park
abstract: Audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) can fail at full-video speech-vision decisions even when useful visual evidence is locally recoverable. We introduce Temporal Evidence Decomposition (TED), a training-free diagnostic framework that separates local visual verification from speech-relative aggregation. title: Towards Human-AI Complementarity for AI Safety
authors: Sander Lanbo Shi, Miranda Anna Christ, Eric Modesitt et al.
abstract: Safely overseeing AI is increasingly challenging for the humans doing it, as they must evaluate longer and more complex outputs with every new model generation.
